title: Identity and Belonging in Adolescence
keyIdea: Your identity is made of many parts: personal traits, values and interests, plus the groups you belong to. Family, friends, media and your own experiences all shape it, and it keeps developing through your teens. Belonging means being accepted as you are; fitting in means changing yourself to be accepted.

kid: Identity is your answer to the question 'Who am I?' Part of it is personal: what you are like, what you care about and what you enjoy. Part of it is social: the groups you belong to, like your family, your year group, a team or a faith. You are all of these at once.

Lots of things shape who you are. Your family passes on language, food and traditions. Friends affect how you dress and talk. Adverts, TV and social media show you what is 'normal' or 'cool'. Your own experiences matter too, like trying drama and finding you love it.

Fitting in and belonging are not the same. Fitting in means changing or hiding part of yourself so a group will accept you, like laughing at jokes you think are cruel. Belonging means people accept the real you. You can be quiet one day and silly the next, and you are still welcome.

Social media can make you feel you are not enough. That is because you compare your normal day with other people's best moments, which are often edited, filtered or paid for. Your identity is also still growing. Changing your interests at 12, 14 or 16 is normal. It does not mean you were fake before.
adult: The PSHE Association's KS3 programme asks pupils to learn about the influences on their identity, how to build self-esteem and a positive self-concept, and how social media can affect self-image. The DfE's 2019 Relationships and Health Education guidance adds healthy friendships and online wellbeing. These questions grow louder at 12 and 13. Around this age, what friends think starts to matter more than what parents think.

Two ideas from psychology help. Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner) says part of how we see ourselves comes from our groups. So being accepted or left out by a group affects self-esteem. Erikson described adolescence as the stage of identity versus role confusion. Trying out interests, friendships and styles is healthy exploration, not a sign that something is wrong.

A common mistake is to treat fitting in as the same thing as belonging. A teenager who hides their culture, faith or interests to stay in a group may look settled. Often they feel lonelier. Another misconception is that identity is fixed, so a change of friends or hobbies feels like losing yourself. A third is upward social comparison: judging your whole life against other people's curated highlights.

The lab follows one invented pupil, Jo. Your child sorts parts of Jo's identity into personal and group rings, traces each part to an influence and judges four moments as fitting in or belonging. They also look behind three polished posts and move along a timeline from age 8 to 16 to see which parts change and which stay steady.

familyTip: Each draw a quick identity web with yourself in the middle: one ring for what you are like, one for groups you belong to. Swap and talk about one thing that has changed since you were younger, and one place where you feel you can just be yourself.

visual.caption: Belonging or just fitting in? Drag each moment, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: Fitting in: changing to be accepted
items: My friends know I am shy and give me time to talk
I pretend to hate a show I love because the group does
I can wear my hijab and still be in the team
I hide my lunch from home so nobody comments
My choir laughs with me when I hit a wrong note
I copy the way the popular kids talk

lab.caption: Flagship lab: map Jo's identity, trace its influences, sort fitting in from belonging, look behind posts and watch identity grow.

practice.prompt: Which of these is part of your social identity?
choices: Being a member of a youth club
practice.hint: Social identity is about the groups you belong to, not what you are like.
practice.explain: A youth club is a group you belong to. Being patient is a personal trait and liking spicy food is a personal taste.

practice.prompt: Tom changes his music taste every time he joins a new group, so people will accept him. What is he doing?
practice.hint: Is he accepted as he is, or is he changing himself to be accepted?
practice.explain: Changing yourself so a group will accept you is fitting in. Belonging is when the group accepts the real you.

practice.prompt: Jo looks at {a} posts. {b} of them were edited or filtered. How many were not edited?
practice.hint: Take the edited posts away from the total.
practice.explain: {a} - {b} = {=a-b}. Even unedited posts usually show a chosen moment, not a whole day.

practice.prompt: Jo draws an identity web with {p} personal parts and {s} group parts. How many parts are on her web altogether?
practice.hint: Add the personal parts and the group parts.
practice.explain: {p} + {s} = {=p+s}. Identity is many parts at once, not one label.

choices: Copying a group so they like you
Being in the most popular group
pool.hint: Do you have to change anything about yourself to belong?
pool.explain: Belonging means a group accepts the real you. Copying others to be liked is fitting in.

pool.prompt: Which is a media influence on identity?
choices: An influencer advert for a skin cream
Your aunt teaching you her recipes
Your best friend's sense of humour
pool.hint: Media means content made to reach many people, like adverts and social media.
pool.explain: The advert is media. The aunt is a family influence and the friend is a peer influence.

pool.prompt: Ana's interests at 15 are very different from when she was 11. What does that show?
choices: Identity keeps developing in the teenage years
pool.hint: Is identity fixed, or does it grow as you try new things?
pool.explain: Exploring new interests is a normal part of adolescence. Her identity is developing, not disappearing.

pool.prompt: Why can scrolling through social media lower self-esteem?
choices: You compare your ordinary life with other people's highlights
Other people's lives really are better
pool.hint: Think about which moments people choose to post.
pool.explain: Posts are chosen, edited and sometimes paid for. Comparing your whole life with them is an unfair comparison.

pool.prompt: Which is part of your personal identity?
pool.hint: Personal identity is your traits, values and interests.
pool.explain: Caring about fairness is a value. Year 8 and the swim team are groups, so they are part of social identity.

pool.prompt: Kai laughs at jokes he thinks are mean so the group keeps him. What would help him most?
choices: Finding people he can be himself with
pool.hint: Is Kai fitting in or belonging right now?
pool.explain: Kai is fitting in by hiding what he thinks. Belonging is easier to find with people who accept him as he is.

pool.prompt: Jo belongs to {g} groups. She leaves {k} of them and joins {j} new ones. How many groups does she belong to now?
pool.hint: Take away the groups she left, then add the new ones.
pool.explain: {g} - {k} + {j} = {=g-k+j}. Groups change through your teens, and that is part of identity developing.

pool.prompt: Out of {t} things Jo says about herself, {v} are values. How many are not values?
pool.hint: Take the values away from the total.
pool.explain: {t} - {v} = {=t-v}. The rest might be interests, traits or groups.
